prompt: The read loop of section 02 got `0 "" EOF` on its fourth call. What was `io.EOF` telling it?
hint: The program printed `done` afterwards.

choices.text: That the read failed and the last bytes were lost
choices.why: The last byte, `o`, arrived on the third call; nothing was lost and nothing failed.

choices.text: That the input was over, the normal way out of the loop
choices.why: Right. It is a sentinel for the end of input, and the loop broke on it and printed `done`.

choices.text: That `buf` was too small for the rest of the string
choices.why: A small buffer only means more calls; the reader filled 4, 4 and then 1 byte.

choices.text: That the string held a byte which was not valid text
choices.why: `Read` does not judge the bytes at all, and `Hello, Go` is plain text.

prompt: Lesson 34 said to prefer `errors.Is`, yet the loop writes `err == io.EOF`. Why is that safe?
hint: Read the parenthesis in `go doc io.EOF`.

choices.text: `io.EOF` is a constant, and constants compare with `==`
choices.why: `go doc` printed `var EOF = errors.New("EOF")`: a variable, like every sentinel.

choices.text: A `Read` method must return `io.EOF` itself, never wrapped
choices.why: Right. The documentation makes that a rule for readers precisely so that callers can use `==`.

choices.text: `errors.Is` cannot find `io.EOF`, because it has no `Unwrap`
choices.why: `errors.Is` checks the error itself first, so it finds `io.EOF` just as well.

choices.text: `==` is faster, and a read loop runs often
choices.why: Speed is not the argument the documentation makes; the guarantee that `io.EOF` arrives unwrapped is.

prompt: `io.ReadAll` reads a reader to its end with no trouble. What error does it return?
hint: Reaching the end was what it was asked to do.

choices.text: `io.EOF`, since the reader returned it
choices.why: The reader did return it to `ReadAll`, which does not pass it on: `A successful call returns err == nil`.

choices.text: `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`
choices.why: That one is for input that stopped in the middle of something; an expected end is not that.

choices.text: `nil`
choices.why: Right. For a function asked to read everything, reaching the end is success.

choices.text: The data, and a joined error holding every `io.EOF` it met
choices.why: It returns one error, and for a successful read that error is `nil`.

prompt: By convention, the name of a sentinel such as `ErrUnexpectedEOF` starts with `___`; `io.EOF` is the exception.
hint: Five of the six in `io` follow it.

prompt: A file format starts with a 16-byte header, and a parser's reader runs out after 9 of them. What should the parser return?
hint: Was this end allowed to happen here?

choices.text: `io.EOF`, because the input ended
choices.why: `io.EOF` says the input ended where it was allowed to; a header cut at 9 bytes did not.

choices.text: `nil` and the 9 bytes, since some data arrived
choices.why: A header with 7 bytes missing is not a result anybody can use; returning `nil` hides a broken file.

choices.text: `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`, or an error with more detail
choices.why: Right. The input stopped in the middle of a structure, which is a failure, and `go doc io.EOF` names this error for it.

choices.text: `io.ErrShortBuffer`, because the buffer could not be filled
choices.why: That sentinel is about a buffer too small for what must go in it, not about input that ran out.

prompt: A package declares its own `var EOF = errors.New("EOF")` and its reader returns that at the end. Does a caller's `err == io.EOF` catch it?
hint: Lesson 33 compared two errors made from the same words.

choices.text: Yes, both say `EOF`
choices.why: Equal words do not make equal errors: two `errors.New` calls make two different values.

choices.text: No: it is a different value with the same message
choices.why: Right. A sentinel is matched by identity, so only `io.EOF` itself is `io.EOF`, and that reader breaks every caller's loop.

choices.text: Yes, because both variables are named `EOF`
choices.why: A name is how code refers to a value; the comparison is between the values, which differ.

choices.text: Only with `errors.Is`, which compares messages
choices.why: `errors.Is` compares values too, link by link, and no link here is `io.EOF`.

prompt: Why does section 03's `main` check `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound)` instead of `err == store.ErrNotFound`?
hint: What did `Count` do with the sentinel before returning it?

choices.text: `==` cannot compare values that come from another package
choices.why: It can; the trouble is which value it gets, not where the value came from.

choices.text: `Count` always returns it wrapped, with the item's name
choices.why: Right. The value `main` receives is the wrapper, so only a check that walks the chain finds the sentinel.

choices.text: `ErrNotFound` is unexported and `==` cannot see it
choices.why: It starts with a capital letter, which is why `main` can name it at all.

choices.text: `errors.Is` also matches any error whose message is `not found`
choices.why: It never reads messages; that is the point of a sentinel being a value.

prompt: `store.Count("pear")` returned 0 and a `nil` error. Why is having no pears not an error?
hint: Think of every caller that would then have to handle it.

choices.text: None in stock is a good answer; an error would make it a failure
choices.why: Right. The store sells pears and has counted them; the count happens to be 0.

choices.text: The map gives 0 for a missing key, so `Count` cannot tell pears from plums
choices.why: The comma-ok form tells them apart, and `Count` uses it: `plum` got the sentinel.

choices.text: A zero value counts as success in Go
choices.why: Nothing in the language says so; `Count` chose `nil` because 0 is a real count here.

choices.text: `Count`'s errors are reserved for items it does not sell
choices.why: A function may return any error; this one happens to have just one failure today.

prompt: Which of these are what make `store.ErrNotFound` usable by a caller in another package? Select all that apply.
hint: One is about naming it, one about knowing when to look for it.

choices.text: Its name starts with a capital letter, so it is exported
choices.why: Yes. Without that, `main` could not write `store.ErrNotFound` at all.

choices.text: `Count`'s comment says its error wraps `ErrNotFound`
choices.why: Yes. The signature says only `error`, so the comment is where a caller learns what to check.

choices.text: Its message is lower case with no full stop
choices.why: That makes the message read well inside a longer one; callers that check with `errors.Is` never read it.

choices.text: It is created by `errors.New` inside `Count` on every call
choices.why: That would make a new value each time, which nothing could match; a sentinel is made once, at package level.

prompt: A second package, `catalog`, also declares `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")` and wraps it the same way. What does `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound)` say about an error from `catalog`?
hint: Same words, same name, different `errors.New` call.

choices.text: `true`, as the two messages are identical
choices.why: `errors.Is` compares values, not text, and these are two values.

choices.text: Nothing: the program does not compile with two `ErrNotFound`
choices.why: Each lives in its own package, `store.ErrNotFound` and `catalog.ErrNotFound`, so the names never clash.

choices.text: `false`, because only `store`'s own variable matches
choices.why: Right. That is exactly what keeps a missing catalogue entry from being mistaken for an item the store does not sell.

choices.text: `true`, because both variables share the name `ErrNotFound`
choices.why: Names are for the code that writes them; at run time only the values are compared.

prompt: In section 03's `switch`, the `case err != nil` line is moved above the `errors.Is` case. What does the program print for `plum`?
hint: A `switch` with no tag runs the first case that is true (lesson 19).

choices.text: `plum: not sold here (count "plum": not found)`, as before
choices.why: The sentinel case is never reached: the error is not `nil`, so the case above it already matched.

choices.text: `plum: failed: count "plum": not found`
choices.why: Right. Every non-nil error matches `err != nil`, so the specific check has to come before the general one.

choices.text: `plum: 0 in stock`
choices.why: The `default` case only runs when no case matched, and `err != nil` did.

choices.text: Nothing: two cases match, so the compiler refuses the `switch`
choices.why: Overlapping conditions are legal in a tagless `switch`; the first true one wins.

prompt: Match each situation to the shape of error it calls for.
hint: Two questions: does a caller branch on it, and does it need data?

pairs.left: Callers stop reading when the input ends
Callers need the line number that was wrong
pairs.right: an error type with a field

pairs.left: Callers only add context and return it
Callers need the kind of failure and the input
pairs.right: an error type that carries a sentinel

prompt: In the `sentinel-v2` run, `Count` stopped wrapping `ErrNotFound`. What changed for section 03's `main`?
hint: Compare the `plum` lines of the two runs.

choices.text: It no longer compiled
choices.why: It compiled, and `go vet` passed; the variable it names still exists.

choices.text: The message for `plum` lost the item's name
choices.why: The message was `count "plum": not found` in both runs, letter for letter.

choices.text: Its `errors.Is` case no longer matched, so `plum` came out as `failed`
choices.why: Right. Same text, no sentinel in the chain, and nothing reported the change.

choices.text: `go vet` warned that `ErrNotFound` was never returned
choices.why: `go vet` found nothing; whether a variable is ever returned is not something it checks.

prompt: Which change to `store` breaks its callers loudly, with a compile error?
hint: One of them made `go run` print `undefined`.

choices.text: Returning the error without `%w`
choices.why: That is the quiet one: it compiled, and the caller's branch simply stopped matching.

choices.text: Deleting the variable `ErrNotFound`
choices.why: Right. `main` named it, so the build failed: `undefined: store.ErrNotFound`.

choices.text: Rewording the message inside `errors.New("not found")`
choices.why: Callers that use `errors.Is` never read the message, so nothing of theirs changes at all.

choices.text: Adding a second sentinel for another failure
choices.why: A new variable breaks nobody; it is a new promise, which is its own cost.

prompt: For `strconv.Atoi("99999999999999999999")`, which of these is true?
hint: The error is a type with a sentinel in its `Err` field.

choices.text: `errors.Is(err, strconv.ErrSyntax)` is true, since that is too long to be an int
choices.why: Every character is a digit, so the syntax is fine; the value is what does not fit.

choices.text: `errors.Is(err, strconv.ErrRange)` is true, and `errors.AsType` gives back the input
choices.why: Right. The run printed `too big for an int` and `Num="99999999999999999999"` for the same error.

choices.text: `err == strconv.ErrRange` is true
choices.why: The outer value is the `*strconv.NumError`; `ErrRange` is one link down, in its `Err` field.

choices.text: `err` is `nil` and `n` is the largest `int`
choices.why: `Atoi` returns an error for a number that does not fit; the run went to the range case.

prompt: An error with a message but no variable or type a caller can check for is called ___, and it is the default.
hint: It is free to change because nobody can depend on it.

prompt: You write `parseConfig`. It can fail on a dozen kinds of bad line, and its only caller prints the error and exits. What should it return?
hint: Does any caller branch on the kind of failure?

choices.text: A sentinel for each kind of bad line, so callers can choose later
choices.why: A dozen promises nobody asked for, each one impossible to take back without breaking somebody.

choices.text: An opaque error from `fmt.Errorf`, with the line in its message
choices.why: Right. Nobody branches and nobody needs a field, so the message for a person is the whole job.

choices.text: One sentinel, `ErrBadConfig`, for all of them
choices.why: Smaller, but still a promise with no caller to keep it for; the one caller only prints.

choices.text: A panic, since a broken configuration cannot be recovered from
choices.why: A bad file is an error a caller should see, not a bug in the program; lesson 36 is about panics.

prompt: Which of these are sentinels? Select all that apply.
hint: A sentinel is a variable holding one error value.

choices.text: `io.EOF`
choices.why: Yes: `var EOF = errors.New("EOF")`.

choices.text: `strconv.ErrSyntax`
choices.why: Yes. It sits in the `Err` field of a `*strconv.NumError`, and `errors.Is` finds it there.

choices.text: `*strconv.NumError`
choices.why: That is an error type with fields, found with `errors.As`; it carries a sentinel but is not one.

choices.text: The `errors.New("age cannot be negative")` inside lesson 32's `price`
choices.why: It is made on each call and kept in no variable, so nothing can match it: an opaque error.

prompt: In the `sentinel-v2` run, how many of the three items were reported as `failed`?
hint: `apple` and `pear` were never errors.

prompt: Put in order what happens to `store.ErrNotFound` on the way to section 03's `plum` line.
hint: It starts before `main` runs at all.
items: `errors.New` makes it once, at package level
`Count` wraps it with `%w` and the item's name
`errors.Is` walks the chain and finds it
